title: Data quality measures and metrics
description:
Define how we know the data is good, and how that is reported — to a maintainer
deciding what to work on next, and to the app, which should be able to say "I do
not know enough about this species to judge it".

Without this, coverage growth is invisible and every rule silently degrades on
thin data while looking exactly as confident as it does on good data. That is
the failure mode already seen once: rule 8 reported soil mismatches with total
assurance while the catalog held no tolerance data at all.
design:
CANDIDATE MEASURES — pick, do not implement all:

  Completeness    % of required fields with a sourced value, per species and per
                  field. The per-FIELD view drives collection priority; the
                  per-SPECIES view drives whether a species can be judged.
  Provenance      % of values carrying a real source. Should be 100% by rule —
                  anything less is a pipeline bug, not a metric.
  Agreement       Where 2+ sources cover a field, how often they agree. A field
                  with chronically low agreement is one to distrust generally,
                  not just on the rows where it was noticed.
  Freshness       Age of the retrieval, per source.
  Adjudication    Count of unresolved conflicts — a work queue, not just a
                  number.
  Confidence      A per-species roll-up: can this species be assessed at all?

CAUTION, from the nl-jsm epic: it decided AGAINST a composite ecology score
because the weights would be invented, and the same reasoning applies to any
single "data quality score". Prefer per-dimension reporting for the same reason.
A completeness percentage is defensible because it is a count. A weighted
quality index is not.

FEEDS THE APP: the four-status enum in src/analysis/ecology.js already has
'not-declared' for "the input this rule needs is absent". Thin data on a species
should route through that existing path rather than inventing a fifth status.
Worth checking whether the rules can currently distinguish "no value" from "a
value that happens to be empty" — if not, that is a finding for the data model.

FEEDS PRIORITIZATION: the metrics ARE the work queue. Design them so
"which species x field pairs are missing and matter most" is a query.
acceptance_criteria:
• A chosen metric set with a stated reason for each, and per-dimension rather
  than a single composite index
• A defined route from thin data to the existing 'not-declared' status, with no
  new status invented
• The metrics expressed as queries the prioritization work can consume
• A check on whether rules can currently tell "no value" from "empty value"
notes: Delivered docs/data-acquisition/05-quality-metrics.md. Six metrics kept separate (completeness per-field/per-species, provenance as a 100%-by-construction tripwire, agreement, freshness, adjudication, confidence roll-up) -- no composite index, per nl-jsm's precedent. Confirmed no fifth status needed: ecology.js's four-status enum already covers thin data via NOT_DECLARED; the gap is upstream (nl-41o.4's export must preserve ABSENT vs ASSERTED-EMPTY) and downstream (nl-c58: 5 of 7 checked fields currently fabricate a default instead of reaching not-declared -- re-read plantParser.js/siteMatch.js/birdFood.js/keystoneGenera.js directly this session to confirm nl-41o.1's measurement still holds). Wrote all six metrics as concrete SQL queries against 04's indexes. Review caught and fixed a real bug in the 'missing' query: an unfiltered CROSS JOIN over taxa double-counts synonym rows as 0%-complete species and under-counts cultivars that inherit unoverridden fields from their parent -- fixed with resolves_to IS NULL and a parent-claim fallback.

title: Conflict resolution and manual corrections
description:
When two sources disagree, what wins — and how does a human override both
without the next crawl silently undoing it?

The second half is the one that quietly fails. A pipeline that re-derives values
from sources on every run will erase a correction someone spent an hour
researching, and leave no trace that it did. Corrections need to be first-class,
durable, and attributable.
design:
TO DECIDE:

  Precedence  Is it a fixed source ranking, per-field (USDA wins on
              distribution, a regional book wins on horticultural judgement), or
              confidence-weighted? Per-field precedence is more work and
              probably more correct — a source authoritative for one field is
              often weak on another.
  Corrections Stored as a claim from source 'manual' with the highest
              precedence? That keeps one mechanism instead of two, and makes a
              correction visible in the same audit trail as everything else.
              Requires a reason and an author, or it is indistinguishable from
              a typo six months later.
  Staleness   A correction made against 2026 USDA data may be wrong after a 2028
              revision. Does a correction pin the source version it was made
              against, and flag when that source changes underneath it?
  Unresolved  Some conflicts should NOT be auto-resolved. Surfacing "these two
              sources disagree and nobody has adjudicated" is more honest than
              silently picking one, and it feeds the work queue. Decide what the
              app shows for an unadjudicated field — probably the same answer as
              a blank: report it as unknown rather than guess.

PRECEDENT IN THE REPO: ecology/host-genera.csv carries a per-row source string,
including one row that records a correction to the source itself (the NWF PDF
prints 'Gridelia'; the row says Grindelia and the source column says why). That
is a correction with a reason attached, done by hand, and it is the pattern to
generalize.
acceptance_criteria:
• A precedence rule, stated per-field where per-field is warranted
• A correction record shape carrying reason, author, and the source version
  it was made against
• A guarantee that a re-crawl cannot silently erase a correction, and a
  described mechanism for it
• A decision on what an unadjudicated conflict shows in the app
notes:
A LIVE CONFLICT TO DESIGN AGAINST, found 2026-08-27 (nl-41o.1) — no longer hypothetical.
GET /api/PlantWildlife/46985 (Callicarpa americana) returns TWO source records that
disagree on the same field for the same species:
  {Source: 'Martin',  LargeMammals: 'Minor',    SmallMammals: 'Minor'}
  {Source: 'Miller',  LargeMammals: 'Moderate', SmallMammals: 'Minor'}
Instructive because it is the HARD kind: neither source is wrong, they are different
studies, and no precedence rule derived from 'which source is more authoritative'
resolves it. Exactly the case the bead flags as one that should NOT be auto-resolved.
Use it as the worked example for the unadjudicated-conflict path.
close_reason: Designed precedence (per-field, derived from 02's PRIMARY/CORROBORATING roles), the manual-corrections.tsv format and replay-last ordering, staleness via pinned retrieved_at + claims_dry_run diff, and the unadjudicated-conflict app behavior (blank export, visible in claims_conflicts). title: A shrunken yard reports stray plants but says nothing about features
description:
outOfBounds() in src/interaction/setupPanel.js filters getPlants() only, so the 'N outside the yard' list counts plants and ignores features entirely. Live in projects/example-frontyard at its saved 6 x 25 ft yard: one plant is reported, and all three features reach past it — the box out to y 31.5 — with nothing said.

Half-consistent rather than wholly wrong, which is the awkward part. 'Scale the whole design to fit' DOES move features, deliberately, because a bed scaled while the plants in it stay put is worse than either alone. But the report they are not in, and 'Move inside the boundary' does not touch them, so pressing it clears a list that was never telling the whole truth.

Fix: count features in the same pass, name them in the same list, and either clamp their points or say plainly that a feature has to be reshaped in Features mode rather than nudged. Clamping a footprint point-by-point deforms the shape, so translating the whole feature back inside is probably the honest move — worth deciding before building.
close_reason: outOfBoundsFeatures() now checks every feature point against yardFt, alongside the existing plant check; both counts merge into one 'N outside the yard' report and one stray list, and the 'Show features' toggle is forced on the same way plants are. A feature is translated as a whole (new translateFeaturesInside in app.js) rather than clamped point-by-point, which would deform the shape. Verified end-to-end in the browser: a trellis reaching past a shrunken yard is now named in the list and, on 'Move all inside the boundary', shifts intact (1.5ft span preserved) rather than collapsing. Updated tests-e2e/yardConflict.spec.js (the scratch project's own backyard-copy trellis was already stray) and added tests-e2e helpers.readScratchFeatures.

Views derive their rect; the photo gets its own originFt/extentFt in yard feet (drag to place, ruler to scale). Drops cropped/detail views (backgroundFrom) but keeps the crop math as photo placement. The assertion should be: guides in every view, handles/ruler in the selected one only. Fails at HEAD, independent of nl-k1k and the mode-pill fix.

title: An elevation has no observer, so a wall behind the camera is drawn in front of the yard
description:
example-frontyard's wall sits at y 21.6, north of the bed. In the south elevation (viewFrom south, farIsHigh true) it correctly sorts far and lands in the background. In the north elevation (viewFrom north, farIsHigh false) it sorts NEAR and is drawn over the plants as a 6 ft band — but the north photo was taken from the walkway south of that wall, so the wall is behind the camera and should not be drawn at all.

The cause is that an elevation models no observer position. Its axis span is authored (originFt.x + extentFt.width) and its ground height is authored (originFt.y), but nothing says where along the DEPTH axis the camera stands, so the camera is implicitly at infinity and everything in the yard is in front of it. Affects every wall and box, in any project, whenever a feature sits between the camera and the yard.

Not a per-feature visibleFrom flag: features are one model projected into every view, and a per-view visibility flag on the feature breaks that.
acceptance_criteria: An elevation may declare where its camera stands along the depth axis; a feature entirely behind it is not drawn; an absent declaration culls nothing; plants are clamped out of that region by resolveYardBounds rather than culled.
close_reason: An elevation may now declare viewerAtFt: where its camera stands, in yard feet, on its DEPTH axis. Absent means cull nothing, so every existing project draws what it drew before; zero is a real position, so the tests are on finiteness. Normalized/serialized in src/data/projectConfig.js (elevations only), carried on the transform, authored in Setup mode as 'Camera stands at (<axis> ft)' with a blank = anywhere. isBehindViewer in src/render/elevationOrder.js culls a feature whose depthFt.FAR sorts nearer than the observer — far, not near, so a fence the camera stands in the middle of is kept rather than half-vanishing — and it goes through compareElevationDepth so north/west (camera at the high end) come out right without a second case. Plants are never culled: resolveYardBounds narrows the depth axis to the observer instead, so a plant cannot be dragged behind a camera and the narrowing shows in the Shared yard readout. Verified in the running app on example-frontyard: with north's camera at y 21 the y-21.6 wall leaves the north elevation and still backs the south one. 12 unit tests across featureViews, yardBounds and projectConfig, all inlined. NOT written into projects/example-frontyard/project.json — the real camera position is a measurement the author has to make, and that file has uncommitted edits of theirs.

title: Setup-mode Save can drop a view's originFt, moving its ground line
description:
projects/example-frontyard/project.json was found with every originFt removed — including the elevations' negative originFt.y, which positions each ground line. Dropping them moves every ground line to the panel's bottom edge. The file is written only by POST /api/project (Setup mode's Save views), so a Save wrote zeros where the loaded config had real offsets.

serializeProjectConfig omits originFt when it is {0,0}, which is correct on its own — the bug is upstream, wherever the in-memory view lost its origin. Suspects: a plan corner-handle drag (resolveHandleDrag rewrites originFt and extentFt together), the ruler calibration patch, or a view edit through the setup form that rebuilds a view without carrying originFt across.

Reproduce: load a project whose elevations have a negative originFt.y, enter Setup mode, edit or drag something, press Save views, and diff project.json. Found 2026-08-20 while working nl-avt.6; the file was restored in commit 9ac0069.
acceptance_criteria: A Setup-mode Save round-trips a view's originFt unchanged unless the user actually moved it; a regression test covers a project with a negative originFt.y.
close_reason:
NOT REPRODUCED as a code defect, and now pinned by tests so it cannot become one silently. tests-e2e/setupSave.spec.js drives a scratch copy of example-frontyard's exact geometry (plan origin {2, 14.83}, north originFt.y -7.14, west -3.20) through: a plain Save views; a form edit on the plan then Save; a form edit on an elevation then Save; and a ground-line handle drag then Save. Every origin round-trips untouched, and the drag moves ONLY the dragged view's origin. The pure round trip normalizeProjectConfig -> serializeProjectConfig -> normalize is stable too, verified separately.

So the flattening was almost certainly a real Setup-mode handle drag: dragging an elevation's ground line to the panel's bottom edge sets originFt.y to exactly 0, and serializeProjectConfig then omits an origin of {0,0} — the tool working, leaving a file that looks like it never had an origin.

The residual risk is real but different from what this bead assumed, and is NOT a serialization bug: view geometry has no undo (project.json keeps no history, deliberately — see nl-avt.5 and persistProjectConfig's comment), so one stray handle drag plus a Save silently destroys a calibrated ground line with no way back. Worth its own bead if it bites again; the cheap mitigations are a confirm on Save when an origin goes to zero, or keeping the previous project.json as a single .bak on write.

Filed originally after I swept the damaged file into commit 9a63b3a with 'git add -A'. Restored in 9ac0069.

title: Persist features through POST /api/features
description: Server endpoint plus the client persistence module, following /api/project exactly: id from the directory rather than the body, resolveProjectPaths for containment, writeJsonAtomic so a crash never leaves a half-written file, and a body that must carry features[] or be refused outright (there is no history to recover from). No undo stack — features are setup, like project.json.
acceptance_criteria: Saving features writes projects/<slug>/features.json atomically and only inside that project; a body without features[] is rejected; server.js changes are deployed with 'docker compose restart web'.
close_reason: server.js GET+POST /api/features, featuresFile in projectPaths.js, loadProjectFeatures/persistFeatures in src/data/persistence.js, boot wiring in app.js, tests/persistFeatures.test.js (5) + tests-e2e/features.spec.js (5, own scratch project 'features-save'). Full unit suite passes; 42/42 e2e. DEPLOYED and verified live: 'docker compose restart web' then curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/features?project=backyard' -> {"features":[]} HTTP 200. Design calls: (1) There is a GET twin, not just the POST the bead asked for, and the app loads through it — fetching features.json off disk logs a console 404 on every load of every project that has never drawn a feature, which app.spec.js:26's console-clean assertion catches. featureConfig.loadFeatures is now static-file-mode only. (2) Missing file reads as {features: []}; a file that exists but is unreadable still throws — absent is normal, corrupt is a fault. (3) POST refuses a body with no features[]: absent means 'this is not a feature list', not 'no features', and accepting it would erase the whole yard model with no history to recover from. An explicit empty array IS accepted — that is how the last feature goes. (4) The response is re-normalized on the client: the drawing reads style and heightFt off every feature, and a response is trusted no more than a file. (5) The e2e containment test posts a body naming a different project and asserts the named one is untouched — worth noting normalizeFeatures never reads raw.id at all, unlike normalizeProjectConfig, so there is no id scrub; the test pins that rather than assuming it. PNG export needed no work: viewCapture.js clones the live SVG (cloneNode + serializeToString), so features come along free. persistFeatures has NO UI caller yet by design — nl-avt.6 owns that. Docs: AGENTS.md gained a 'Yard features' section and CLAUDE.md was mirrored per the repo rule. Non-blocking for .6: app.js passes no status callback to loadProjectFeatures, so a corrupt features.json degrades to an empty yard with only a console.warn — the author sees no features and no reason why.

title: Plan-only shape editor: select, move, vertex drag, add, delete
description:
The single biggest scope saver: features are edited in the PLAN view only. Footprints live in plan space, and a height is a number in a form field, not a drag — so elevations stay derived and read-only.

Reuse createSetupController's proven pattern rather than inventing a second interaction model: pointer capture, rAF-throttled repaint, MIN_HITBOX_RADIUS_PX for touch, and a candidate reported through onChange for the app to validate before it becomes live. MVP is select, move, drag a vertex, add a rect or line, delete, reorder — then stop. This is an app inside the app and it is where scope quietly triples.
acceptance_criteria: A feature can be drawn, moved, reshaped, and deleted in the plan; every elevation updates from the same model; a rejected edit leaves the drawing on the last good state.
close_reason:
src/render/featureOverlay.js (pure geometry: handles, hit-test, drag resolution, new shapes, reorder), src/interaction/featureController.js (pointer), src/interaction/featurePanel.js (list + form), plus a fourth mode in app.js/index.html/styles.css. tests/featureOverlay.test.js (9) + 3 UI tests in tests-e2e/features.spec.js against their own scratch project 'features-edit'. Full unit suite passes; 45/45 e2e with every pre-existing spec UNMODIFIED. No deploy needed: server.js is untouched and src/index.html/styles.css come off the bind mount.

Design calls: (1) A FOURTH mode, not a modifier on Setup. setRuler is a modifier on one gesture; feature editing has its own selection state and would have made three consumers competing for pointerdown on one SVG. applyMode decides every lock state in ONE place so exactly one kind of controller is ever unlocked. (2) Feature controllers are built ONLY for plan panels (null for elevations, index alignment kept) — a controller on an elevation would be a consumer that never unlocks. (3) Handles are drawn in EVERY plan view, not just one selected view. That differs deliberately from Setup mode's one-view rule: setup edits a single view's geometry, features edit a model shared by all of them, so editing from a detail crop is coherent. The pointer goes through transform.viewBoxToPlan, so a drag in a crop still writes YARD feet — unit-tested. (4) createFeatureShape gives a new wall/box a real heightFt. normalizeFeatures refuses one without a positive height, and the first frame of a new fence must not be what trips a guard meant for malformed files. (5) applyFeatureEdit normalizes the candidate DIRECTLY rather than serializing first — a freshly added shape has no style yet, and normalizeFeatures is what supplies one. (6) NO auto-save: features are setup like project.json, per this epic's own framing, so Save features is explicit. A plant drag auto-saves; this deliberately does not. (7) The panel got its OWN BEM block (feature-panel__*). Reusing setup-panel__* made four existing e2e specs fail on strict-mode ambiguity — two panels, one class name, and a selector for one silently matches the other. styles.css carries both hooks on every shared rule so the visual language stays single-sourced.

Known limits, none blocking: a polygon collapsed to zero area cannot be re-picked on canvas (pickFeatureAt ignores the touch radius for polygons, using pointInPolygon) — the panel list is the escape hatch. Type is not editable on an existing feature: surface/box are a polygon and wall is a path, so switching would need the footprint rebuilt; delete and re-add. Vertices can be dragged but not added or removed, so a bed stays a quadrilateral — worth its own bead if curved beds matter. nl-jfm updated: svg.style.cursor now has three writers.

title: features.json schema, normalize, and serialize
description: Yard features are geometry in FEET shared across every view, so they get their own file rather than living in project.json. Three primitives: surface (flat, zero height), wall (extruded path), box (extruded polygon). Styles are authored in feet (strokeWidthFt) so a feature keeps its weight when a view is rescaled. Mirror projectConfig.js: reject non-finite coordinates, supply style defaults, drop defaults on write.
acceptance_criteria: normalizeFeatures rejects malformed input loudly and round-trips through serializeFeatures unchanged; ids are validated slugs; unit tests cover each primitive.
close_reason: src/data/featureConfig.js + tests/featureConfig.test.js. Design calls made here that .2/.3/.5 inherit: (1) heightFt THROWS for wall/box rather than defaulting — a zero-height wall renders as nothing in an elevation, the exact silent failure 'reject loudly' exists to catch; a surface may not carry a heightFt at all. (2) Absent file == empty list: normalizeFeatures(null|{}) -> {features: []}, no 'declares no features' throw, so an empty POST in .5 is valid. (3) normalize/serialize are exact inverses ({features} both ways, no projectId echo); the round-trip is tested as normalize(serialize(normalize(x))) deepEqual normalize(x), since serialize drops defaults. Both directions read one defaultStyle(type) table. (4) Only the geometry key matching the type is emitted — footprintFt for surface/box, pathFt for wall — so projection in .2 cannot read the wrong one. (5) style.fill/stroke restricted to hex, a colour name, or none, since they land in SVG attributes and arrive over an endpoint in .5. Also added projectFeaturesPath() and loadFeatures(); featuresFile in projectPaths.js is left to .5.

title: Project a feature into plan and elevation views
description:
Pure projection module. Plan: footprint vertices through transform.planToViewBox. Elevation: footprint projected onto the view's horizontal axis via axisToX, vertical from heightToY(baseFt) to heightToY(baseFt+heightFt), producing a crude silhouette rectangle. Also reports the feature's extent along the view's DEPTH axis for sorting.

Everything goes through viewTransform and resolveElevationOrientation. Doing the subtraction in feet by hand is wrong for the mirrored north/west views and wrong on the vertical axis everywhere.
acceptance_criteria: A parity test per compass direction, mirrored included, matching the style of tests/elevationOrientation.test.js. No trigonometry or axis arithmetic outside viewTransform/elevationOrientation.
close_reason: src/render/featureProjection.js + tests/featureProjection.test.js (projectFeature dispatches; projectFeatureToPlan/ToElevation do the work). All four compass directions are pinned by absolute expected pixels, not only by mirror parity, so a bug shared by both sides of a pair cannot hide. Design calls .3 inherits: (1) The axis span is taken in PIXELS after axisToX, never in feet — on a mirrored view the larger axis value gives the smaller x, so a min/max in feet puts the rectangle's left edge on its right. (2) TWO degenerate silhouettes are legitimate, not errors: a surface has height 0 by definition, and a wall seen end-on (a fence running away from the viewer) has width 0. The renderer must draw both at strokeWidthPx or a fence vanishes in two of four elevations. (3) depthFt reports {min,max,near,far}; near/far come from orientation.farIsHigh so compareElevationDepth composes with the plant sort. BUT near is NOT a sufficient sort key on its own: a house spanning y 12..20 sorted at near=12 draws in front of a plant at y=15 that stands inside its footprint. Single-key sorting cannot be right for an extended footprint — .3 has to split or clamp. (4) closed=false for wall only; closing a fence would fill in the yard behind it.

title: Render features, interleaved with plants by depth in elevations
description:
Plan: features beneath plants, array order is z-order. Elevation: features and plants sorted TOGETHER far-to-near, so a fence in front of a plant hides it — the payoff that makes this epic worth building.

This is the one part that is not purely additive: renderViews currently sorts plants alone (orderTopViewPlantStates for plan, elevationViews for the rest) and must sort one combined list for elevations. Layering per view, bottom to top: sky colour, photo (if visible), ground fill, features+plants, overlays. Features draw ABOVE the photo so tracing works.
acceptance_criteria: A feature nearer the viewer than a plant occludes it in the elevation; the same two render in the documented order in the plan; existing plant render tests still pass.
close_reason:
src/render/featureViews.js (shapes), src/render/elevationOrder.js (the combined sort), + wiring in topView/elevationViews/renderViews and tests/featureViews.test.js. tests/topView.test.js and tests/elevationViews.test.js pass UNMODIFIED; 37/37 e2e. Design calls: (1) Plants and features go through ONE comparator with ONE depth accessor — a parallel per-kind expression is how features silently sort at depth 0, pinned to the very back or very front, which looks almost right. The test asserts the straddle order AND notDeepEqual against the depth-zero ordering. (2) An extended footprint is drawn WHOLE at its nearest edge, no splitting: correct for a box (nothing is planted inside a house), and the one case it gets wrong is a wall running away from the viewer, which is edge-on and therefore a hairline. (3) Bands: 0 = surface (flat, so it is ground and draws beneath every plant), 1 = plants and wall/box, 2 = the pre-existing Callirhoe force-front, moved verbatim from elevationViews. (4) SVG draws neither a zero-width nor a zero-height rect AT ALL, so both degenerate silhouettes become a <line> at stroke weight — without that a surface and an end-on fence are simply invisible. (5) No data-name on feature groups: styles.css gives '.view svg [data-name]:hover' a pointer cursor, and features are not interactive until .6, which hit-tests data-feature-id.

HANDOFF TO nl-avt.5: the app is wired end to end EXCEPT the load. renderViews takes options.features and appState.features exists, so .5 is a one-line assignment — but .5 must add a GET /api/features twin returning {features: []} for a missing file. Fetching features.json straight off disk is NOT viable at boot: Chrome logs the network 404 to the console itself, before any try/catch runs, and tests-e2e/app.spec.js:26 asserts boot is console-clean. That was caught by running the e2e suite. loadFeatures' 404-to-empty branch is now only for pure static-file mode.

title: Decide whether the yard has an extent separate from what a view covers
description:
Since nl-tz7.3, drag clamping uses each view's own originFt + extentFt. That fixed an upper-bound bug (the east elevation used to allow y=29.63, which rendered at 880px on an 800px viewBox) but introduced a lower bound below zero: the east elevation's originFt.x is -2.96, so a plant can be dragged to y=-2. The plan view starts at originFt {0,0}, so that plant renders at cy=654 on a 600px viewBox and disappears from the plan.

Views legitimately extend past the yard — an elevation's near-edge inset is margin, not plantable ground. So a view's extent is the wrong thing to clamp plant positions to. Either clamp every view to a shared yard extent, or accept per-view clamping and make the plan view show out-of-bounds plants somehow.

This is the same question nl-tz7.6 / nl-tz7.7 must answer when the setup UI lets someone move a view's origin under existing plants.
design: RESOLVED: clamp every view to a shared yard extent, not to the view's own rectangle. src/render/yardBounds.js resolveYardBounds(views) = the first plan view's rectangle, intersected with the axis range of the first elevation for each compass direction; later views of either kind are detail callouts and do not constrain (a plant outside a zoomed detail is not lost). An empty intersection falls back to the plan view rather than an inverted clamp range. Both drag controllers take an optional getBounds and fall back to the per-view extent when it is absent, so they still work standalone. Rejected alternative: keep per-view clamping and mark out-of-bounds plants in the plan — it leaves the plan lying about where a plant is. Checked both repo layouts against the new bounds: projects/backyard is entirely inside (bounds come out identical to the plan extent, and the old y=-2 hole in the east elevation is closed). projects/example-frontyard has one row, holly-corner at y=25.278, that sits 0.278 ft past the west elevation's 25 ft reach, so it snaps in by ~3 inches the first time it is dragged. That is the rule working: the plant is currently invisible in the west elevation. Left the data alone.
acceptance_criteria: A plant cannot be dragged into a position where it vanishes from another view. Whichever way it is resolved, the rule is stated in AGENTS.md alongside the axis/mirror table.
notes: OPEN QUESTION FOR THE USER (not a code bug): projects/example-frontyard's west elevation covers y 0..25 while its plan covers y 2..27, so the two disagree about the yard's north edge by 2 ft. holly-corner sits at y=25.278, outside the shared bounds, and will snap in by ~3.3 in the first time it is dragged (an ordinary undoable 'Moved plant' history entry). Left the data alone deliberately: widening the west view's extent or shifting its origin would slide its background photo out of alignment, and only the person who authored that photo knows which is right. Fix either by re-authoring the west view to cover y 2..27 or by nudging holly-corner to y<=25.
close_reason: Shared yard bounds implemented in src/render/yardBounds.js and consumed by both drag controllers via a new getBounds option; rule documented in AGENTS.md under Elevation orientation > Yard bounds; tests/yardBounds.test.js covers the near-edge margin, the narrowing elevation, detail views, the non-overlapping fallback, and a plan view with a non-zero origin.

title: backgroundFrom — crop a shared photo to a detail view's rectangle
description:
A crop view sets backgroundFrom: '<viewId>' instead of its own background, reusing the full plan photo cropped to its rectangle. Implemented in src/render/viewConfig.js as background-size / background-position arithmetic.

This is NOT the naive origin/fullExtent*100. CSS background-position: X% aligns the IMAGE's X% point with the CONTAINER's X% point, so the denominator is the leftover travel:

  sizeX% = full.extentFt.width  / crop.extentFt.width  * 100
  sizeY% = full.extentFt.height / crop.extentFt.height * 100
  posX%  = (crop.originFt.x - full.originFt.x) / (full.extentFt.width  - crop.extentFt.width)  * 100
  posY%  = 100 - (crop.originFt.y - full.originFt.y) / (full.extentFt.height - crop.extentFt.height) * 100

posY is inverted because plan y grows north while CSS y grows down. Both denominators are zero when the crop equals the full extent — guard and fall back to 0%. A crop must set background-size explicitly per panel; it cannot inherit the 100% 100% stretch at styles.css:876.
acceptance_criteria: A crop view with originFt {4,9} / extentFt {8,6} / backgroundFrom 'plan' shows exactly that patch of the plan photo, with the plants drawn over it landing on the same features they do in the full plan view. Unit test on the percentage math including the equal-extent guard.
notes:
Start here. The arithmetic is already worked out in the plan doc (~/.claude/plans/help-me-plan-for-jiggly-dragonfly.md) and is NOT the naive origin/fullExtent*100 — CSS background-position aligns the image's X% point with the container's X% point, so the denominator is the leftover travel:
  sizeX% = full.extentFt.width / crop.extentFt.width * 100
  posX%  = (crop.originFt.x - full.originFt.x) / (full.extentFt.width - crop.extentFt.width) * 100
  posY%  = 100 - (same with y)   // plan y grows north, CSS y grows down
Both denominators are zero when the crop equals the full extent — guard and fall back to 0%. styles.css sets background-size: 100% 100% on .view, so a crop must set background-size explicitly per panel rather than inherit the stretch.

Consumer is configureViews in src/render/viewConfig.js, which already resolves backgroundFrom's target by id (validation for an unknown id landed in nl-tz7.2). setupPanel.js already exposes a 'Borrow background from' select.
close_reason: New src/render/backgroundCrop.js resolves a view's background image and, for a backgroundFrom detail view, the patch of it to show. Consumed twice: viewConfig.js sets background-size/-position on the panel (and clears both when a view stops borrowing, since panels are reused by id), and app.js passes the same rect to captureViewToPng as a sourceRect so the exported PNG shows the same patch instead of the whole photo stretched. The crop is derived by mapping the detail's corners through the SOURCE view's transform, which handles mirrored elevations and the plan y-flip for free. normalizeProjectConfig now rejects backgroundFrom across differing type/viewFrom, and the Setup panel only offers compatible sources. tests/backgroundCrop.test.js covers the worked example, the equal-extent and full-width guards, and both mirrored and unmirrored elevations. title: Setup overlay and handle controllers — grid, crop rect, ground line, near edge
description:
New src/render/setupOverlay.js (guides drawn into the selected view's SVG) and src/interaction/setupController.js (handle dragging), both on top of viewTransform.js.

  - foot grid plus a dimension readout
  - plan/crop views: a draggable rect with 8 handles -> originFt / extentFt
  - elevation views: a draggable ground line -> originFt.y, and a draggable near-edge line -> originFt.x

Reuse the patterns dragController.js already establishes: pointer capture, rAF-throttled re-render, setLocked, a generous hit radius (MIN_HITBOX_RADIUS_PX = 28). Rect-handle and line-handle controllers should land around 100-150 lines each. If that balloons past ~300, interact.js is the sanctioned fallback — it is small, SVG-capable, and sits beside dragController.js rather than replacing it. Do NOT reach for a canvas library.
acceptance_criteria: Dragging the east elevation's ground line moves it live and plants' feet track it, no reload. Dragging a crop rect's handles updates originFt/extentFt and the numeric form in step. Overlay guides never appear outside Setup mode. tests/setupOverlay.test.js covers the guide geometry using tests/helpers/fakeDom.js.
notes: originFt.x is the axis value at the view's NEAR edge, not the left edge. For mirrored directions (north, west) axisToX maps originFt.x to viewBox.width — the right-hand side. The draggable near-edge line must read/write against the mirrored edge for those two directions, or it will be built backwards. The plan doc's inline comment ("axis value at left edge") is only true for south/east. See createViewTransform in src/render/viewTransform.js and its inversion test.

Implements 11 (all sections) and 10 section 6.

IT IS A RANKING SIGNAL, NEVER A GATE (10 section 2.1's three-layer structure). It joins the existing rank tier alongside npsot_dfw_recommended, commercial availability and keystone membership, and does not restrict the plantable set. 10 section 6 places it LAST in that tier, as a tie-breaker.

A yard whose nearest anchor is a stream leans riparian/woody; one near a prairie-adjacent cemetery or park leans herbaceous prairie.

The join column is water_pref (11 section 3), chosen because it is the one column that exists on BOTH sides of the plantable set. 11 section 6 settles that this needs no new stored lookup structure.

Scale honesty, per 10 section 2.1: county presence is county-grained; the flora's nativity read is NCTX-region-grained over ~40,000 sq mi. - The signal is labelled a heuristic wherever it surfaces

comments.author: John Syrinek
comments.text:
Investigated, NOT implemented — blocked on a false premise in the bead, not an unsettled weight.

Doc 11 (docs/data-acquisition/11-anchor-kind-prioritization.md) settles every algorithmic
choice cleanly: join column is water_pref (§3), kind→lean mapping (§4), tie handling — skip
the boost when the overall-minimum distance is shared by >1 kind (§2), position last in the
rank tier as a tie-breaker (§5), no new persisted lookup (§6). Nothing there needs a human
call.

The blocker: "it joins the existing rank tier" has no referent in code. Doc 10 §2.1 lists
four other rank signals (npsot_dfw_recommended, USDA Commercial Availability, keystone-genus
membership, already-planted) as the tier anchor-kind is supposed to join, but none of the
four is implemented anywhere — grepped tools/ and src/analysis/ (including
tools/claims/claimsStore.js, exportPlantsCsv.js, claimsTools.js, stoppingCondition.js,
humanViews.js, and every src/analysis rule) and found no species-level ranking/scoring
function at all. src/analysis/ in fact carries a repeated, deliberate "no composite score"
stance (nl-3hi hard boundary — see ecology.js:16, yardRelevance.js:17, rarity.js:21,
plantMatches.js:23, faunaMatches.js:20, localFaunaSupport.js:11) for the app's suggestion
UI, which is a different ranking concept from doc 10/11's collection-priority tier and
doesn't supply a hook either.

So acceptance criterion 1 ("ranking output changes with a project's nearest-anchor kind") is
unsatisfiable as written — there is no ranking output today for anchor-kind to change. AC 2
("labelled a heuristic wherever it surfaces") is vacuous for the same reason: nothing
surfaces it yet, and doc 11 §5/§7 write as if a consumer already exists ("ahead of whichever
future collection pass actually reads this ranking") without naming one.

This needs a human decision among:
1. Split out a predecessor bead that builds doc 10 §2.1's tier (signals 1-4) as a real
   function first; nl-scx.11 stays scoped to anchor-kind and depends on it.
2. Fold tier construction into nl-scx.11 itself, with anchor-lean as signal 5 — substantially
   bigger than a P3 "wire in one column" bead, and it also requires picking the ranking's
   consumer/output (a CLI report? a new claims_* MCP tool? a plants.csv export column? the
   app's suggestion path in src/analysis, which currently refuses composite scores on
   principle?).
3. Ship anchor-lean as a small, tested, standalone module (nearest-anchor kind ->
   water_pref bucket boost, tie-skip, heuristic-labelled) with no wiring into a consumer yet,
   and amend the acceptance criteria to match — buildable today but leaves both ACs
   technically unmet until something reads it.

Recommend (1) or (2) — the hidden sub-decision inside (2) (what the ranking output actually
is and who reads it) is exactly the kind of open design fork this task was told not to guess
on. Left the bead open (unclaimed back via `bd update nl-scx.11 --status open`) rather than
guessing.

No code changed; no commit made.

title: Source soil tolerance for the 34 plants.csv species USDA has no characteristics record for
description: nl-9a6 migrated 23 of plants.csv's 56 species to a measured soil_pref accepted set using USDA's soil_coarse/medium/fine triple. The other 33 (native-passionflower, fragrant-sumac, pink-turks-cap, frostweed, giant-ironweed, horseherb, golden-groundsel, blackfoot-daisy, four-nerve-daisy, bouvardia, arrowwood-viburnum, rock-rose, blue-mistflower's genus-mate Conoclinium greggii, nuttall-sensitive-briar, mealy-blue-sage, aromatic-aster, green-milkweed, antelope-horns, flame-acanthus, narrowleaf-coneflower, undaunted-ruby-muhly, chile-pequin, texas-bluebonnet, standing-cypress, stiff-goldenrod, prairie-penstemon, narrowleaf-gayfeather, leavenworth-eryngo, angularfruit-milkvine, fineleaf-fournerved-daisy, topeka-coneflower, narrowleaf-snakeherb) came back with only profile-level fields (usda_symbol/scientific_name/growth_habit/native_status) and no characteristics record at all when fetched via usda_fetch_details — confirmed not a fetch bug, just absent from USDA's ~2,200-species characteristics coverage. These 33 keep single-value soil_pref (a bare preference) and stay under rule 8's soil caution stopgap in siteMatch.js. A second source (e.g. a regional extension service's soil-tolerance tables, or manual literature review) would be needed to give them real accepted sets.
notes:
2026-09-19: a 34th species joins this set. Silphium albiflorum (white rosinweed, USDA symbol SIAL, plant id 39823) was added to plants.csv and planted in example-frontyard this session. usda_fetch_details returned profile-level fields only -- usda_symbol, scientific_name, growth_habit (Forb/herb), native_status (L48:N) -- and no characteristics record, so no soil_coarse/medium/fine triple exists to build an accepted set from. Same cause as the original 33, confirmed the same way (a live fetch, not an inference from HasCharacteristics, which the search endpoint reports as false regardless -- see 06 section 2).

It differs from the original 33 in one way worth recording: those 33 kept a single-value soil_pref that nl-9a6 could not widen, whereas this row's soil_pref ('clay') was sourced from the NCTX flora treatment at p. 404 ('Calcareous soils, open areas and prairies; Blackland Prairie and Grand Prairie') rather than from USDA at all. It is still a bare preference, not a measured tolerance set, so it sits under rule 8's soil caution stopgap exactly like the other 34 -- but a second source did supply it, which is evidence that the flora can fill soil where USDA cannot. Worth testing that route against the other 33 before reaching for an extension service's tables.

Its water_pref is BLANK for the same underlying gap, so it is also the first row exercising rule 8's 'declares no water preference and was not checked' path in a real project.

title: Revisit the PLANTS mnemonic: continuity and horticultural fit are missing
description:
Owner's own observation 2026-09-16, parked for later - do not act without them.

The rules engine already computes two things the mnemonic has no letter for:
 - bloomSuccession.js - floral continuity across the season, which is the BEE half of the argument (the critique's point that percent-native rewards woody and undercounts floral resources)
 - birdFood.js - fall and winter fruit
And a third the owner raised: HORTICULTURAL FIT - do not waste water and resources on species that do not match the site. siteMatch.js already computes it.

So the engine covers things PLANTS misses, and PLANTS covers things the engine has no surface for (L, A, N, S - all management and behaviour rather than plants). They are complementary; the mnemonic may need a letter for continuity and one for fit.
Owner said they may revise the mnemonic. Their call, their wording - this issue only records that the gap is real and which existing rules already compute the missing pieces.

title: STAGE 5: let local knowledge promote candidates to anchors
description:
No dataset knows which green space is real habitat - see the EMST trap and the OSM fairground in the research issue. Local knowledge is the only source for this, which reframes ASK 02 into a far better ask: not 'does a yard registry exist' but 'which of these candidate anchors are actually habitat', answerable by a chapter room in ten minutes.

Needs a review/promotion path: candidates from public data, promoted (or rejected) by a named human, with the judgement recorded and attributed - consistent with the repo convention that a judgement call says so and says whose it is.

title: Add Bradford/Callery pear to the avoid list
description:
dfw-avoid-non-natives.csv has 12 rows and covers privet (Ligustrum japonicum, L. vulgare), chinaberry (Melia azedarach) and nandina (Nandina domestica) - three of the four woody invasives named in the PLANTS mnemonic. Pyrus calleryana (Bradford / Callery pear) is MISSING.

Needs the same full column set as the other rows (USDA symbol, growth habit, native status, invasive_status_elsewhere, etc). Use the usda-plants MCP tools the way the other rows were sourced.

NOTE: the existing list is BROADER than the mnemonic's four examples - half of it is grasses (Cynodon dactylon, Sorghum halepense, Bothriochloa ischaemum x2, Arundo donax). Do not let the mnemonic's woody examples narrow it.
close_reason: Added Pyrus calleryana (Callery/Bradford pear, USDA symbol PYCA80) to dfw-avoid-non-natives.csv with the full column set, sourced via the usda-plants MCP tools (usda_search_by_name + usda_fetch_details) the same way the other 12 rows were built. invasive_status_elsewhere (Alabama:Category 2; Delaware:Invasive; Maryland:Tier 2; Missouri:Invasive (DOC, IPC); North Carolina:Invasive) came from USDA's per-plant PlantInvasiveStatus/{id} endpoint, the one the README (nl-wwq) documents as the working per-state source. Verified all 13 rows still parse cleanly via parseCsv.

title: Add a second Lepidoptera host source so a blank means absent twice (Decision 5c)
description:
Data work, separate from 5(b). Add a second independent host compilation so an empty FNCT host column can be read as 'absent from two sources' rather than 'absent from one 1999 book'.

Candidates:
 - HOSTS database (Robinson et al., Natural History Museum London) - global lep host compilation, far larger, same agricultural/showy bias
 - Shropshire & Tallamy 2025, Lepidoptera of North America annotated list (Pensoft, peer-reviewed, county-resolved) - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12676573/

The Shropshire & Tallamy county-resolved dataset is also the correct replacement source for the Level I PDF counts generally (see the NWF headline bug).

title: AGENTS.md describes soil_pref as a single preference; the code treats it as a set
description:
Documentation trails the code. AGENTS.md 'Plant Data (CSV)' lists soil_pref among plain single-value species fields, and the rule 8 section says 'Soil is set membership, not a scale' without saying the column itself holds a comma-separated LIST.

The code has been ahead of the doc for a while: siteMatch.js checkSoil splits soil_pref on [,/|] and tests membership, and the regional CSVs use it that way — 'sandy,loamy,clay' appears on 196 of 469 rows in blackland-prairie-natives.csv. Only plants.csv still holds single values, which is what makes the doc look right.

Fix the AGENTS.md description of soil_pref to say it is an accepted-soil SET, comma separated. Worth doing alongside the migration in the soil-stopgap bead, since that is what makes plants.csv match the documented shape.

Raised in docs/data-acquisition/01-goals-and-required-fields.md section 7.
close_reason: Updated AGENTS.md: soil_pref is now documented as a comma-separated accepted-soil set (matching checkSoil's [,/|] split-and-membership-test in src/analysis/rules/siteMatch.js), not a single-value field. Noted plants.csv itself still needs the nl-9a6 migration to match.

title: mapCharacteristics reads 26 of the 81 characteristics USDA returns
description:
MEASURED for nl-41o.1: a full characteristics fetch for Quercus shumardii (plant Id 70468) returns 81 characteristics. tools/usda-plants/mapCharacteristics.js consumes 26 of them. Several of the unmapped ones answer questions the app already asks or was told it could not answer.

Already in the response, currently discarded:
  Commercial Availability     'Routinely Available'  -> suggestion ranking; recommending an unbuyable plant wastes the slot
  Fruit/Seed Persistence      'No'                   -> sharpens rule 7 directly; today winter food is INFERRED from a month range
  Toxicity                    'None'                 -> front-yard fitness
  Lifespan                    'Long'                 -> longevity
  Vegetative Spread Rate      'None'                 -> 'will it take the bed?'
  Seed Spread Rate            'Slow'                 -> reseeder risk
  Resprout Ability            'No'                   -> aggressiveness
  Growth Rate                 'Moderate'             -> establishment expectations
  Height at 20 Years, Maximum '35' (vs mature 100)   -> arguably a better number for rule 11 than mature height

This is the cheapest coverage win available in the whole data epic: no new source, no new licensing, no new requests — the bytes are already being fetched and thrown away.

CAVEAT, and it is why this is P3 not P2: the fields above were sampled on ONE species, a well-studied oak. Confirm they are populated broadly before relying on any of them — that check is already on nl-41o.9's probe list.

Also note mapCharacteristics.js collapses water with 'Moisture Use || Drought Tolerance', discarding the bracket. The two together give a range (drought tolerance behaves as a lower bound, moisture use as an optimum); either alone does not. Recovering that is free and belongs in the same pass.
close_reason: Widened mapCharacteristics.js to capture 9 previously-discarded USDA characteristics as raw columns, added matching probe.js target fields for the broad-population check the bead's own caveat calls for, and fixed the Moisture Use/Drought Tolerance water_pref collapse (was a cross-scale fallback that could invert the value). Broad-population confirmation itself deferred to a probe run, noted on nl-scx.2 which this unblocks.

title: Two plants.csv values fall outside the vocabularies the code accepts
description:
Found while auditing field vocabularies for nl-41o.1. Both are single rows today and both scale badly.

1. fruit_load: 'low' — normalizeFruitLoad (src/data/plantParser.js) recognises none/sparse|light/moderate|medium/heavy|abundant. 'low' matches nothing and falls through to '', which is indistinguishable from blank. birdFood.js then weights it ?? 1 = sparse. So the row is graded, just not on what it says.

2. soil_pref: 'clay-loam' — checkSoil (src/analysis/rules/siteMatch.js) splits on [,/|] only, so 'clay-loam' stays one token and never matches site soil 'clay'. Rule 8 raises a caution against a plant that is fine on the site.

Either extend the accepted vocabulary or fix the two rows. Prefer the vocabulary: the regional CSVs are 469 and 61 rows and will bring more variants.

Related: nl-41o.6's note records that several fields cannot distinguish absent from empty at all, which is the general form of (1).
close_reason: Extended the vocabulary rather than editing the two catalog rows, per the bead's own preference (regional CSVs will bring more variants): normalizeFruitLoad now accepts 'low' as a sparse synonym, and checkSoil expands the compound texture 'clay-loam' to also match a site declared as plain 'clay' or 'loamy' via a small SOIL_COMPOUND_EQUIVALENTS table. Added regression tests in tests/plantParser.test.js and tests/ecology.test.js.

title: Rules 9 (drifts) and 12 (mature-size spacing)
description:
Deferred from the first pass. Both are computable from data already in hand and would drop straight into the analysis registry - no new data, no schema change.

Rule 9 drifts: clump counts and nearest-neighbour from layout x_ft/y_ft. A finding is already waiting - example-frontyard is nearly one-of-everything (17 plants across 12 species, largest clump 3), against the 5-10+ the rule wants. backyard concentrates properly (64 plants, largest clump 19).

Rule 12: width_ft versus neighbour distance.

Ask before building - the user scoped the first pass to 6/7/11/4/10/5/8.
notes:
CROSS-REF CORRECTED 2026-08-27. nl-41o.3's notes claimed the book corpus would
un-defer this bead by supplying mature width. MEASURED FALSE: the NCTX flora is
a taxonomic flora and gives HEIGHT only ("Shrub or small tree to 10 m tall").
Spread is not a character it treats.

Standing position across the whole source inventory: USDA publishes no
width/spread/crown among its 81 characteristics (width_ft is 0% filled across
all 469 rows of blackland-prairie-natives.csv, consistent with there being no
field to map); NPIN gives height-only prose; the NCTX flora gives height only.
NO CATALOGUED SOURCE PUBLISHES MATURE WIDTH. It needs a horticultural book --
in-copyright, purchase-required, none in hand.

This bead stays deferred, and is now blocked on ACQUISITION, not on extraction.
See docs/data-acquisition/03-document-corpus.md §8.
close_reason: Shipped rules 9 (drifts) and 12 (mature-size spacing) in src/analysis/rules/{drifts,matureSpacing}.js, wired into the RULES registry, documented in AGENTS.md. Rule 9: union-find same-species clustering at 1.5x combined canopy radius, thresholds gap<5/partial 5-9/ok>=10 largest clump. Rule 12: cross-species-only overlap check on DECLARED width_ft, severity mild/real/hard. Verified against real project data: example-frontyard largest clump 3 (gap), backyard 17 (ok), matching the plan's own survey numbers -- now locked in as a regression test. Commit 2c7309f.

title: A yard narrowed to a corner by a short elevation raises nothing at boot
description:
resolveYardConflicts uses a strict overlap test, so it only fires when a primary elevation misses the plan entirely. example-frontyard, after nl-cgn, overlaps everywhere and raises nothing — yet its shared yard is x 0-9.37, y 0-14.35 out of a 29.89 x 30.31 plan, about 15%. The consequences are the same shape as the disjoint case, one notch less severe: the traced bed in features.json (x 11.45-20.27) is entirely outside the plantable yard, blackfoot-b at x 12.0 is outside it, and the east elevation draws no plants at all because all five sit at y 14.833 and its far edge is 14.349.

Setup mode now reads the rectangle out (describeYardBounds, nl-cgn), so an author editing geometry sees it. Someone just loading the page does not.

Note this may not be a code bug at all: the 9.37 ft and 14.35 ft extents came from the author's own Measure-a-known-length drags on those photos, and if either measurement is wrong the fix is re-measuring, not code. Decide that first.
acceptance_criteria: Either the extents are re-measured and the shared yard covers the planted area, or a yard much smaller than its plan is surfaced to a viewer, not only to an author in Setup mode.
notes: Also: a plant already sitting behind a newly-authored viewerAtFt is neither culled (plants never are) nor moved (the depth clamp only binds new drags), and since it is still inside the view's axis range it draws at nearest depth — on top of everything. Same visible symptom the wall bug had, with a plant. Reachable today on example-frontyard: set south's camera to 20 and all five plants at y 14.833 are behind it. Not a new class — they are already outside bounds.y.max of 14.349 — but the depth axis turns the failure from quiet (off-canvas) into loud (drawn in front).
close_reason: Not expressible any more. Every view's rectangle is derived from one declared yardFt (nl-t08), so no elevation can narrow the shared yard — resolveYardBounds returns the yard itself and resolveYardConflicts is gone. The concern that survived was the yard being typed smaller than the planting standing in it, which is nl-urc: the Setup panel names what falls outside and offers scale-to-fit or move-inside.

title: example-frontyard's west elevation covers a y range the plan does not
description:
resolveYardBounds narrows the plan's rectangle by each primary elevation's axis range. In projects/example-frontyard, the plan covers y 14.83..45.14 while the 'west' view (viewFrom east, axis y) covers y 0..14.35 — the two do not overlap at all, so the inverted range falls back to the plan and the west elevation can draw none of the shared yard.

Consequences are not specific to features: a plant dragged inside the shared yard is invisible in that elevation too, and a newly added yard feature lands off its canvas however it is placed. Found while fixing nl-avt.6's 'new feature not visible in other views' report — the general fix (anchor and size new shapes to resolveYardBounds) leaves this one project's west elevation unfixable because no yard coordinate is in both.

Either the project's geometry is wrong (its west elevation was authored against a different origin) or resolveYardBounds should report a non-overlapping view rather than silently falling back. AGENTS.md calls example-frontyard a throwaway template, so fixing the config is probably right.
acceptance_criteria: A coordinate inside resolveYardBounds is drawable in every primary view of example-frontyard, or the app says which view disagrees.
close_reason: Reported rather than repaired. resolveYardConflicts (src/render/yardBounds.js) returns each primary elevation whose axis range does not intersect the plan's; app.js shows it in #projectNotice at boot. For example-frontyard: 'View "west" covers y 0–14.3 ft, but the plan covers 14.8–45.1 ft — nothing in the yard can appear in both.' The geometry itself is NOT rewritten: the correct coordinate is one the author has to choose and the app cannot measure it, so guessing would silently move someone's yard. resolveYardBounds keeps its silent fallback on purpose — a drag needs some bound — the conflict is now surfaced alongside it. 2 unit tests in tests/yardBounds.test.js, including that end-to-end touching is not overlapping. Note the app's own touch-action/cursor precedent: this is the same shape of bug, a silent fallback that looks like it worked.

title: Hide a view's photo once its features are traced
description:
Upload a photo, position it against the yard, trace the house/fence/bed edges over it, then toggle the photo off or leave it on. The photo becomes a tracing aid rather than the deliverable — accurate feet-based geometry, with the picture still available when showing the plan to someone.

Most of this has landed, and not the way this issue assumed. Calibration is no longer 'the existing ruler': the ruler is gone (under a declared yard it no longer solved a view's extent), and a photo is placed by dragging it and pulling an aspect-locked corner in Setup, which also widens the drawing so a picture larger than the view can be reached. Features are drawn in Features mode on the plan, and Setup already has a Show features toggle over the positioned photo — so tracing works today.

What is left is the last clause: hiding the photo OUTSIDE Setup. A per-view flag (photoHidden, say) that configureViews honours when it sets the CSS background, so a finished drawing can be shown as clean feet-based geometry. Small, and no crop math involved — the placement stays exactly where it is, it just is not painted.
acceptance_criteria: A view with both a photo and features can show either or both; hiding the photo leaves the drawn yard intact and needs no crop math.
close_reason: Added photoHidden per-view flag: normalize/serialize round-trip, Setup checkbox, and configureViews honors it for the CSS background outside Setup

title: Sky and ground fill as per-view properties
description:
Sky is not a shape and modelling it as one feels wrong immediately. Sky and ground fill are per-view presentation, so they belong on the view in project.json (skyColor / groundColor) alongside label and background — not in features.json, which holds yard geometry only. Ground fill paints below the view's ground line; sky paints above it.

Note since nl-t08: the band below the ground line is no longer per-view either. It is elevationFt.below, one number for the project, which is what puts every elevation's ground on the same row of the page. So groundColor paints exactly that shared band and skyColor the elevationFt.above one — the fills stay per-view, the geometry they fill does not.
acceptance_criteria: A view can declare skyColor/groundColor, they survive a Setup-mode save, and a view that declares neither renders exactly as it does today.
close_reason: Implemented skyColor/groundColor as per-view properties

title: A borrowed background crop assumes the source photo fills its viewBox
description:
cropToCssBackground emits background-size as a percentage of the CONTAINER (1/cropWidth), which presumes the source photo covers the whole panel. Since backgrounds are now painted 'contain', that presumption is false whenever a source photo's aspect differs from its view's aspect: the photo letterboxes, but the crop still scales as if it did not, so a backgroundFrom detail view shows the wrong patch.

Pre-existing rather than introduced — under the old 'background-size: 100% 100%' the same mismatch stretched the source photo, so the crop rectangle was equally wrong, just wrong in a different way. Only correctly-authored sources (photo aspect == view aspect) are unaffected, which is why projects/backyard and example-frontyard's street-bed detail are fine and the crop tests pass.

Fix means letting the crop math account for the letterbox: compute the photo's drawn rectangle inside the panel from the photo's intrinsic aspect vs the view's, then express the crop relative to that rather than to the container. Needs the photo's intrinsic dimensions, which nothing currently loads.
acceptance_criteria: A detail view borrowing from a source whose photo aspect differs from its view aspect shows the same patch of yard on screen as in the exported PNG.
close_reason: Both halves are gone. backgroundFrom and detail callouts were removed with nl-t08, so nothing borrows a photo to crop; and the assumption underneath — that a source photo fills its viewBox — no longer has to be assumed, because app.js now loads each background's intrinsic aspect into photoAspects and containPhotoFt derives the drawn rectangle from it (nl-0di). placementToCssBackground expresses an explicit rectangle rather than inferring one.

title: Uploaded backgrounds are orphaned if the user never saves views
description:
POST /api/view-background writes the photo to disk immediately, but the view's 'background' path only reaches project.json when Setup mode's Save views runs. Upload a photo, then close the tab without saving, and the file stays in projects/<slug>/img/ with nothing referencing it. supersededBackgrounds only collects earlier uploads for a view when a NEW upload to that same view succeeds, so an abandoned file is never collected.

Not urgent — the files are small (well under 1 MB) and a later upload to the same view does clean up. Options: sweep unreferenced img/<view-id>-<hash> files on project save, or upload to a staging name and promote it on save.

Still true after nl-t08 and nl-0di, and one notch more likely: positioning a photo is now something you do at length before saving, so there is more room to walk away mid-way.
acceptance_criteria: Uploading a background and then abandoning the session leaves no file that nothing references.
close_reason: Fixed: POST /api/project now sweeps content-addressed uploads no view's background path still references, right after writing config. New orphanedBackgrounds() in src/data/backgroundStore.js, wired in via removeOrphanedBackgrounds() in server.js. Tests added. Commit 1bd51c2.

title: example-frontyard is both a shipped test fixture and the user's live project
description: Repo tests pin geometry and plant ids in projects/example-frontyard, but the same project is editable in the running app: Setup-mode Save rewrites project.json and a drag rewrites planting_layout.csv. On 2026-08-20 a Save dropped the 'street-bed' detail view, breaking tests/projectConfig.test.js and the crop e2e spec; the layout CSV was curated at the same time, removing rockrose-bed. Move the multi-panel/crop coverage onto the scratch fixture (tests-e2e/scratch-fixture.mjs already builds a throwaway root) or onto a project that is not user-editable, so ordinary use of the app cannot fail the suite.
acceptance_criteria: No test in tests/ or tests-e2e/ asserts on geometry or plant ids that live in a project the user edits through the UI. Editing example-frontyard in the app and saving leaves npm test and npm run test:e2e green.
close_reason: Both shipped-project tests moved off user-editable projects. tests/projectConfig.test.js now uses inline fixtures (LEGACY_BACKYARD for the migration parity test, PLAN_WITH_DETAIL for the crop-config test) — what was under test was normalizeProjectConfig all along, so the input belongs beside the assertions. The e2e crop spec moved onto a new 'detail-crop' scratch project whose fourth-view geometry is owned by tests-e2e/scratch-fixture.mjs. No test in tests/ or tests-e2e/ now asserts on geometry or plant ids from a project the user edits through the UI.

title: Verify the long-press clone/remove menu on a real touch device
description: The context menu opens on the native contextmenu event, which on touch means long-press. CDP's Input.dispatchTouchEvent does not synthesize contextmenu, so tests-e2e/touch.spec.js cannot cover it either way — a hold delivers only pointerdown/pointerup/click. Two things worth checking on an actual phone: whether long-press still reaches the menu now that the SVG is touch-action:none in Edit mode, and whether handlePointerDown's event.preventDefault() suppresses it when the press lands on a plant. Not a known break; unverified. The touch route to Clone/Remove is covered: a tap in View mode opens the detail sheet, which carries both.

title: Drag and feature controllers both write svg.style.cursor
description:
Same shared-element bug as the touch-action one fixed earlier (several controllers own the same SVG and the last writer wins), but for cursor. applyMode unlocks the drag controller (cursor: grab), then syncSetupOverlay/syncFeatureOverlay run and reset it. Cosmetic only; touch-action was fixed by giving each controller its own class, and cursor wants the same treatment.

Two writers left, not three. setupController stopped claiming a resting cursor with nl-t08's follow-up — it now sets only the cursors it owns outright (a resize over a photo corner or a camera, grab over the photo, grabbing while dragging) and returns 'default' at rest. dragController and featureController both still write svg.style.cursor unconditionally in setLocked and release:

  src/interaction/dragController.js — 'grabbing', and 'default'/'grab' by lock state
  src/interaction/featureController.js — 'grabbing', 'grab', 'move', restingCursor()

Whatever fix lands has to cover both, and the class-per-controller precedent is right there in styles.css for touch-action.
notes: Now three writers, not two: src/interaction/featureController.js (nl-avt.6) also sets svg.style.cursor — in setLocked, release, and updateHoverCursor — and a plan SVG carries drag + setup + feature controllers. touch-action was handled correctly for the third one (is-features-enabled, mirroring the existing class-per-controller fix); cursor was not. Whatever fix lands has to cover all three.
close_reason: Fixed: cursor now driven by is-drag-enabled/is-features-enabled CSS classes; each controller only sets inline cursor for its own transient states and clears it with removeProperty

title: Emptying a layout discards its history on reload
description: persistLayout now accepts an empty plants array, so removing the last plant does reach disk. But loadLayoutHistory -> findHistoryEntryIndexByLayout returns -1 for an empty layout CSV (it bails on a blank string), so the next page load reports 'History diverged from planting_layout.csv' and throws the history stack away. Degrades quietly; only reachable by removing every plant.
close_reason: Does not reproduce on current code: buildLayoutCsv always emits a header row even for zero plants, so an emptied layout's CSV is never blank and findHistoryEntryIndexByLayout matches the last (empty) entry correctly. Verified end-to-end against a live server (scratch project, real persistLayout/loadLayoutHistory round trip). Added a regression test in tests/persistence.test.cjs to lock this in.

title: Setup mode authors feet; viewBox is derived
description:
Resolved the open question in the plan doc's Design section 8 ('derive viewBox from extentFt — decide when building bead 6').

The first cut of the setup form locked extentFt to the viewBox's aspect ratio, so typing a height silently rewrote the width — you could never say '30 ft by 10 ft'. Wrong value derived.

Now extentFt is authored freely in both directions and viewBox = extentFt * a per-view resolution (px per ft). Aspect ratio is whatever the extent says, and the non-uniform view createViewTransform rejects is unreachable from the form rather than merely guarded against. The two pixel fields collapsed into one 'Resolution (px per ft)' knob, with the derived drawing size shown as a hint.

normalizeProjectConfig and serializeProjectConfig still read and write an authored viewBox, so hand-edited project.json files are unaffected.
acceptance_criteria: Setting Width (ft) then Height (ft) leaves both at what was typed; covered in tests-e2e/app.spec.js.
close_reason: Landed with the drag-coverage commit.

title: Upload background images through the UI
description:
DEFERRED from nl-tz7. Setup mode expects background images to be dropped into projects/<slug>/img/ by hand, with the relative path typed into the form. A file-picker upload endpoint would remove that step.

Needs multipart handling in server.js (which is currently JSON-only), an allowlist of image types matching MIME_TYPES, a size cap, and the same path-traversal guard resolveProjectPaths already applies.
notes:
Follow-up 2026-08-20, reported against the shipped feature: an uploaded photo was distorted. Root cause was pre-existing — .view painted backgrounds 'background-size: 100% 100%', which scales a photo differently on each axis whenever its aspect differs from the view's. It stayed invisible because every projects/backyard photo is 800x600 against an 800x600 viewBox.

Fixed in styles.css by painting 'contain' instead, and by capping the panel's WIDTH rather than its height (width: min(100%, calc(70vh * var(--view-aspect-ratio)))) — with width:100% a max-height constrains both axes, drops aspect-ratio, and reintroduces the stretch. Per the user's instruction the photo does NOT reshape the view: extentFt is untouched by an upload.

The crop branch in viewConfig.js sets background-size explicitly and was deliberately left alone; see the follow-up bead about backgroundFrom crops under letterboxing.
close_reason: Closed

title: Yard feature drawing (beds, hardscape, house footprint)
description:
DEFERRED — deliberately out of scope for the Viewport Setup Mode epic (nl-tz7), and nothing in that epic blocks this.

Beds, borders, hardscape, house footprint, paths, and existing trees are yard geometry in FEET shared across every view — different in kind from per-view presentation config, so they do not belong in project.json. They get their own file, projects/<slug>/features.json, their own render module drawn beneath plants, and their own endpoint.

Rendering a feature into an elevation reuses viewTransform / resolveElevationOrientation, so the mirror/offset math stays in exactly one place. Depends on nl-tz7.1 landing viewTransform.js.
design:
APPROACH: one yard model in FEET, projected into every view — never a drawing per view.

Drawing a background per view is the cheap version and it is a trap: the house
gets drawn three times, the three disagree, and it buys nothing on occlusion.
One model projected everywhere is where all the leverage is, and it is what the
original description already calls for.

Accept the conceptual cost up front: this is a small 2.5D model, not a drawing
tool. Every feature carries a FOOTPRINT and a HEIGHT, because it has to appear
in both a plan and an elevation. That is the part that bites during design
rather than during coding.

--- PRIMITIVES (three is enough for a real yard) ---

surface  flat, zero height: driveway, sidewalk, gravel bed, lawn, bed outline.
         Plan: filled polygon. Elevation: a thin band at ground level across
         its axis span.
wall     an extruded line: fence, retaining wall, garden edge.
         Plan: a thick line along its path. Elevation: a rectangle from base to
         base+height over its axis span.
box      an extruded polygon: house, shed, raised planter.
         Plan: the footprint. Elevation: a silhouette rectangle spanning its
         axis extent, base to base+height.

Silhouettes are deliberately crude rectangles. That is the point — this is the
in-app version of the 3-to-5 <rect> SVGs example-frontyard already ships.

SKY IS NOT A FEATURE. Sky and ground fill are per-view presentation, not yard
geometry, so they belong on the view in project.json (skyColor / groundColor),
not in features.json. Modelling sky as a shape will feel wrong immediately.

--- SCHEMA: projects/<slug>/features.json ---

{
  "features": [
    {
      "id": "house",              // slug, unique, same pattern as view ids
      "type": "box",              // surface | wall | box
      "label": "House",
      "footprintFt": [ {"x":0,"y":28}, ... ],   // polygon, yard feet (wall uses pathFt)
      "baseFt": 0,                // ground height at its base; lets a feature sit on a step
      "heightFt": 22,             // omitted/0 for surface
      "style": { "fill": "#e8e4dc", "stroke": "#c9c3b8", "strokeWidthFt": 0.1 }
    }
  ]
}

Strokes are authored in FEET like everything else, so a feature keeps its
weight when a view is rescaled. Normalize/serialize mirrors projectConfig.js:
reject non-finite coordinates, default the style, drop defaults on write.

--- PROJECTION (the crux) ---

Plan:      map each footprint vertex through transform.planToViewBox. Direct.
Elevation: project the footprint onto the view's horizontal axis to get
           [axisMin, axisMax], map both through axisToX; vertical runs from
           heightToY(baseFt) to heightToY(baseFt + heightFt).
Depth:     a feature's extent along the view's DEPTH axis, for sorting.

Go through viewTransform and resolveElevationOrientation for every one of
these. Do NOT do the subtraction in feet by hand — north and west are mirrored
and yard y grows north while image y grows down. AGENTS.md's axis/mirror table
is the authority and the parity tests in tests/elevationOrientation.test.js are
the template.

--- DRAW ORDER: a refinement of this epic's original design ---

The description says "drawn beneath the plant layer in every view". That is
right for a PLAN and wrong for an ELEVATION.

Plan:      features beneath plants, always. Sorted among themselves by array
           order (authoring order is the z-order).
Elevation: features and plants INTERLEAVED, sorted together far-to-near by
           depth. This is the whole payoff — a fence at y=30 with height 6
           actually hides the plant behind it, which the photo approach could
           never do without per-pixel depth.

That interleave is the one integration point that is not purely additive:
renderViews currently sorts plants alone (orderTopViewPlantStates for plan,
elevationViews for the rest). It has to sort one combined list for elevations.

Full per-view layering, bottom to top:
  1. sky colour (view-level)
  2. photo background, if the view has one and it is visible
  3. ground fill below the ground line (view-level)
  4. features + plants, interleaved by depth in elevations; features under
     plants in plan
  5. overlays — setup handles, ruler, labels

Features sit ABOVE the photo, which is what makes tracing work.

--- WHAT THIS REMOVES ---

* Calibration. A drawn-only view needs none: you author in feet, so pxPerFt is
  already known. "Measure a known length" stays, but only for photo views.
* Detail crops. A drawn view re-renders its vectors at its own extentFt — no
  crop rectangle, no background-size percentages, no drawImage source rect.
  nl-8f9 is irrelevant for drawn views, and backgroundFrom stays photo-only.
* The occlusion problem that made the perspective/photo option open-ended.

--- EDITOR SCOPE: edit in the PLAN view only ---

The single biggest scope saver, and it is well justified: footprints live in
plan space, and a height is a number in a form field, not a drag. Elevations
are DERIVED and read-only.

MVP: select a feature, move it, drag a vertex, add a rect/line, delete,
reorder. Reuse createSetupController's proven pattern — pointer capture, rAF
throttle, MIN_HITBOX_RADIUS_PX, candidate reported through onChange for the app
to validate. Do not invent a second interaction model.

--- AUTHORING FLOW: the hybrid, and the reason to build this at all ---

  upload a photo -> calibrate it with the ruler -> TRACE the house, fence, and
  bed edges over it -> toggle the photo off (or leave it on)

The photo becomes a tracing aid rather than the deliverable. Tracing over an
already-calibrated photo is a far better gesture than drawing blind in feet,
and it directly answers the "authoring views is fiddly" complaint that started
this. Needs a per-view photo visibility flag; everything else already exists.

--- RISKS ---

* Editor scope creep. This is an app inside the app. Ship the smallest
  primitive set that draws the real front yard, then stop.
* Undo. There would be three stacks (layout has one, project config has none).
  Simplest honest answer: no history for features, same as project.json.
* Curves. Polygons only in v1; a curved bed is approximated with vertices.
* Sloped ground. baseFt handles discrete steps. True slopes are out of scope
  and should stay that way.
* Persuasiveness. Crude shapes convince a person less than a photo does. This
  is the one axis where photos genuinely win, and it is exactly what the
  photo-underlay hybrid is for.

--- TESTING ---

* Projection is pure: unit-test it like backgroundCrop and yardBounds, with a
  parity case per compass direction including the mirrored ones.
* Any e2e that saves features must use the scratch fixture and take its OWN
  project in SCRATCH_PROJECTS — a spec pointed at a project not in that list
  silently falls back to the default and asserts against the wrong yard.

--- NOT DOING ---

Perspective rendering. It breaks the uniform-pxPerFt invariant that
viewTransform.js enforces, turns pxPerFt into pxPerFtAt(point) across ~20
callers, forces backgrounds out of CSS into canvas for screen and export
alike, and leaves depth/occlusion against photo content open-ended. This epic
gets the eye-level-ish result people want at a fraction of the cost, and keeps
the coordinate system that makes plant SIZE meaningful (topView.js draws a
plant at toPx(plant.width)/2 — feet are what make the drawing answer "will this
fit").
